articles.headline: Editorial : Formation: la valeur des chemins différents
articles.dek: Editos by Benoit Dubuis · Oct 14, 2026

blocks.alt: Editorial : Formation: la valeur des chemins différents

blocks.text: Je suis souvent surpris par le besoin qu’ont certaines personnes ayant suivi des parcours de formation nouveaux, parallèles ou alternatifs de justifier leur choix en dénigrant les voies dites « traditionnelles ». Comme si, pour donner de la valeur à une école nouvelle, il fallait nécessairement qualifier les autres d’écoles de grand-papa, sclérosées, incapables de comprendre un monde qui change. Cette opposition me paraît aussi inutile que pauvre. Une formation de base solide reste essentielle. Elle ouvre les yeux, donne des repères, construit un langage, permet d’intégrer ensuite de nouvelles connaissances et, surtout, de comprendre les enjeux auxquels on sera confronté. Certains acquerront cette capacité autrement, bien sûr. D’autres ne l’acquerront jamais, quel que soit le diplôme obtenu. Mais cela ne retire rien à la valeur d’une formation exigeante et structurante.

Cela ne signifie évidemment pas que les institutions historiques doivent rester figées. Elles doivent évoluer avec leur temps, adapter leurs contenus, leurs méthodes, leurs interfaces avec le monde professionnel et répondre à des besoins qui changent. Mais elles doivent aussi rester exigeantes. Lorsque vous entrez dans une école polytechnique ou une faculté de médecine, vous savez que vous allez devoir travailler dur. On attendra beaucoup de vous, mais on vous donnera aussi énormément. Cette exigence n’est pas un défaut du système ; elle en est une composante essentielle. Une institution exigeante demande à l’étudiant d’être lui-même exigeant envers lui-même. Et cette discipline, cette capacité à apprendre, à raisonner et à remettre son travail sur le métier font partie de ce que l’on emporte bien après avoir oublié une grande partie du contenu des cours.

Dans un autre registre, la Fondation Inartis a accompagné la naissance et le développement de l’École 42. Son modèle est radicalement différent. Son ambition aussi. Pour certains, elle constituera une formation initiale ; pour d’autres, un complément, une reconversion ou un approfondissement. Je ne peux que saluer et soutenir cette démarche. Mais je me garderais bien de chercher à la placer au-dessus ou au-dessous d’une autre institution. J’avais d’ailleurs été très déçu, lors de son inauguration, par le refus d’un ancien président de haute école d’y participer au motif que l’on ne pouvait comparer 42 à son institution. Précisément : on ne devait pas les comparer. Toute la richesse de 42 était ailleurs, dans sa complémentarité, dans sa manière différente d’apprendre et dans les profils différents qu’elle pouvait révéler. La condescendance d’une institution historique à l’égard d’un nouveau modèle me paraît donc aussi déplacée que le discours inverse consistant, pour certains étudiants de ces nouvelles écoles, à construire leur identité contre les hautes écoles classiques.

Nous sommes différents par nos parcours, notre maturité au moment où nous faisons nos choix, nos compétences, nos aspirations, nos contraintes et parfois simplement par les rencontres qui ont jalonné notre chemin. La véritable richesse d’un système de formation n’est donc pas de désigner une voie supérieure aux autres, mais d’offrir de la diversité et, surtout, des passerelles entre institutions, entre formations et entre moments de vie. Une formation professionnalisante n’est pas une formation de base, pas davantage qu’une formation académique ne prépare à elle seule à tous les gestes d’un métier. Elles répondent à des fonctions différentes. C’est précisément pour cela qu’elles ont besoin les unes des autres.

Au fond, la finalité de la formation devrait être beaucoup plus simple : donner à chacun le bagage nécessaire pour devenir très bon dans ce qu’il fait, y trouver sa place et, si possible, y être heureux. Nous avons besoin d’excellents médecins, ingénieurs, développeurs, techniciens, artisans, chercheurs, entrepreneurs, infirmiers ou designers. Le but n’est pas d’être moyen dans un domaine auquel on ne correspond pas, mais d’exceller dans celui où nos capacités et nos aspirations peuvent pleinement s’exprimer. C’est pourquoi je me méfie lorsque de nouvelles écoles se présentent comme des « alternatives » aux anciennes. Ce faisant, elles réduisent parfois elles-mêmes leur propre singularité. Elles n’ont pas besoin d’exister contre quelqu’un. Elles ont simplement besoin d’être excellentes dans ce qu’elles apportent de différent.

Et puis, il faut remettre le diplôme à sa juste place. Il est souvent une clé d’entrée. Il ouvre une porte, crédibilise un socle de compétences, permet parfois simplement d’accéder à un entretien. Mais une fois la porte franchie, ce sont notre personnalité, notre capacité à apprendre, notre jugement, notre engagement et nos compétences réelles qui font la différence. La clé est importante. Ce qu’elle résume est peu de chose par rapport à ce que nous sommes.

…et là se trouve ce qu’un système de formation mature devrait chercher à produire : non pas des diplômés convaincus que leur chemin était le seul valable, mais des personnes suffisamment formées pour comprendre la valeur des chemins qu’elles n’ont pas empruntés.
Source : Republic of Innovation — https://republic-of-innovation.ch/editorial-formation-la-valeur-des-chemins-differents/

articles.headline: Funny numbers
articles.dek: OpenAI’s revenue mix-up, and the dotcom habit of inventing metrics

blocks.alt: A desk calculator seen from above

blocks.text: I started my career in the dotcom bubble, and the dotcom bubble had a lot of funny numbers. There were metrics that people didn’t really understand or didn’t mean much, like ‘hits’, bandwidth or the number of hosts on the internet. There were also carefully created new ‘adjusted’ metrics that avoided all the stuff you didn’t want to talk about. My personal favourite was the new entrant mobile operator that started talking to investors about EBITDA before customer acquisition: the main costs for the business were capex and customer acquisition, so ‘EBITDA before CAC’ was effectively ‘revenue’. There were a bunch of jokes at the time about how the next metric would be ‘earnings before costs’.
We’re seeing a lot of the same stuff this time around. We don’t really know what metrics would be best, we don’t have the metrics that we would like anyway, and the metrics we do have are… funny.
[Paywalled — the rest of this Premium column continues for subscribers at the source: https://www.ben-evans.com/newsletter]
OpenAI’s revenue number

Late last month, Axios and other media outlets reported that OpenAI’s annualised monthly revenue had passed $70bn. This week, it emerged that this was a mistake and the actual number was ‘close to $50bn’. The confusion seems to be that in general OpenAI has been reporting revenue net of payments to companies that resell its models (Microsoft, AWS) where Anthropic has been reporting gross, and both OpenAI and investors were also trying to gross-up the numbers to make them comparable, without making it clear which numbers they were using when leaking to the media.
See this week’s column (Premium).

articles.headline: A Landmark Study of Our Immune System Aging With A Promising Blood Test
articles.dek: A Tale of Two T Cells: GZMK+ vs GZMB+ memory cells and what they mean for healthspan

blocks.text: In the journal Immunity a paper with an obscure title was published on October 9th, 2026. It was entitled “Single-cell analyses of global cohorts outline determinants of immune aging and link the ratio of GZMK+ to GZMB+ Tem cells to health trajectories,” which I think is one of the worst titles I have ever seen for, ironically, one of the most important papers in the science of aging. I still don’t understand why authors and journal editors use or allow such arcane titles!

In this edition of Ground Truths I’m going to unpack the extraordinary work done by the team led by Maxim Artyomov. It takes our understanding of how our immune system ages—both healthily and unhealthily—to a new level with practical implications for determining its status, and promoting our healthspan.
This turns out to be a tale of two cells—different subtypes of memory T cells—that contain distinct types of granules resulting in divergent functions. And, importantly, major health outcomes.

blocks.caption: Schematic Figure made with the help of ChatGPT

blocks.text: Phase 1: Massive Single-Cell RNA Sequencing
Some very impressive stats for who was studied and what was done:
—8 international cohorts, 2,609 individuals, 12,394,834 white blood cells
—age 18 to 98 years
—59 immune cell types from sc-RNA seq harmonization

The story starts with the thymus gland, which starts to involute in early life and accelerates after puberty, after which there is progressive loss of naive T cells and recent thymic emigrants (RTEs) with ageThis decline was the strongest predictor of chronological age in the study. The problem is not so much that the naive T cells, the “rookies,” are declining but what is coming in, as the immune system adapts, to replace them—the “veterans.”

Until this study, prior cell sorting (flow cytometry) or pooled sequencing methods could not differentiate CD8+ effector memory T cells. That was only enabled by obtaining single-cell transcriptomes at scale.

The 2 types of veterans are effector memory T cells (Tem) that are either mainly granzyme K or B. You can think of the B is “bad,” since these cells are leaky, exhausted, and spilling of their granules leads to dissolution of matrix, disruption of tissue, activation of macrophages, and inflammation. That profile of the terminally differentiated GZMB+ cells was characterized from experiments in mice. The bifurcation (Figure below) is influenced towards GZMB+ by cytomegalovirus (CMV) exposure and chronic diseases, such as cardiovascular (CVD) or metabolic (such as Type 2 diabetes).

blocks.caption: The 2 paths that the naive T cells can differentiate to as the rookies become veterans. The path to GZMB+ is influenced by CMV and chronic diseases. Figure made with combination of Google Gemini and ChatGPT

blocks.text: Phase 2: High-Throughput Proteomics

Doing single-cell RNA seq at scale to correlate with clinical outcomes or for development of a clinically useful blood test is not practical, not to mention expense. Instead, using the Olink assay of thousands of plasma proteins in 4 independent cohorts (of the 8 used in Phase 1) per cent TemB+ (Tem stands for T effector memory cell) correlated the best with the single cell GZMB+ data (using a LASSO computational model). That protein signature was tightly correlated with the single-cell RNA-seq work, as seen below in each of the 4 cohorts.
Note: Throughout this post please recognize the interchangeability of terms established between GZMB+ and TemB+, or GZMK” and TemK+.

Then TemB+ was validated for clinical outcomes in the UK Biobank in 48,620 participants with 17-year follow-up, using both the cell protein data. As you can see below, individuals with a high per cent TemB+ had a much higher all-cause mortality than those with low % Tem B+ or the average group, as categorized in tertiles. The x-axis is years of follow-up.

blocks.caption: Figure made with help of Google Gemini

blocks.text: The TemB+ % was predictive of multiple specific health outcome as shown below.

In contrast, however, note the lack of any predictive correlation with neurodegenerative diseases and macular degeneration : Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, dementia, and age-related macular degeneration.
To emphasize the contribution of viral exposure and inflammation, the people who were seropositive for CMV had higher GZMB+ and those with higher C-reactive protein had higher % TemB+
Here is a simplified dichotomy of clinical outcomes and inflammaging based on high Tem B+% (or GZMB+).

blocks.caption: Figure made with help from Google Gemini

blocks.text: Of course there are plenty of limitations. The patients in the multiple cohorts were predominantly of European and Asian ancestry, leaving some uncertainty as to whether the findings will extrapolate to those of African ancestry. The window into immune cell aging was purely via blood cells, not tissue. “TemB+ was measured at a single time point, so we don’t know how it changes within a person, or whether lowering it changes the risk. Importantly, the dichotomy of the “good” and “bad” TemK+ and TemB+ cells, respectively, is an over-simplification, since we know K cell granules can also promote inflammation. CD*+ T cell counts weren’t available in the UK Biobank so they had to be imputed with a model. None of this work is establishing causality. I have not gotten into the “weeds” of the report, which is a beast to read and unravel, and there is much more about different types of cells, other mouse experimental data, Type 2 immunity remodeling, and so on.
Implications

This is a seminal paper, the most comprehensive assessment of white blood cells across the human lifespan that tracks immune cell aging and its relationship with survival and multiple adverse health outcomes. Let me break it down to the key points:
1. Primacy of the thymus gland . The study identified the decline in naive T cells and recent thymic emigrants as the basis of the aging clock, predicting chronological age.

2. It’s not just that we lose naive T cells as the thymus involutes, but it’s about the type of cells that come in to replace them . And it turns out there’s a critical bifurcation between TemK+ and TemB+ cells. The difference in the granules of these cells can account for inciting or fostering inflammation. Extensive characterization of the TemB+ cells from mice showed their propensity to be leaky, exhausted, and tissue disruptive.

3. Viral exposure, most notably by CMV blood positivity , affects the bifurcation path to promote TemB+ cells.. The other main influence on promoting TemB+ instead of TemK+ were chronic diseases, notably cardiovascular and metabolic.

4. The discovery in the work using single-cell RNA sequencing in >12 million white blood cells of the bifurcation and link to outcomes might not have been made with traditional methodologies of cell sorting, flow cytometry, or pooled sequencing. This is yet another reinforcement of getting “granular” (no pun intended with granules) with respect to learning from single-cell data.

5. A new protein blood test emerges from this body of work, the percent of TemB+, or ratio of TemB+ to TemK+. It might be considered a master indicator of unfavorable immune system aging. This could lead to a simple and inexpensive window into a person’s immune status and the researchers in the current study are indeed pursuing that goal. For people found to have an unfavorable immune status, we know of ways that can be improved with lifestyle factors and vaccines, and much more will be done in the years ahead to find other means.

6. Here in late 2026 we have no way of assessing a person’s immune system in the clinic , as I’ve previously written on “ Why We Need an Immunome.” Ironically, we have so many ways to control the immune system, releasing its brakes (t hink immune checkpoint inhibitors and ten other classes of interventions ) and B-cell depletion or “inverse” vaccines to induce tolerance in autoimmune conditions. We can dial it up or down but can’t measure it! In recent months we have seen 2 new practical ways to get at this crucial assessment: (1) AI analysis the thymus gland from a low resolution chest CT (See “Your Thymus and Your Healthspan” ) and (2) Proteomic clocks of the immune system and immune cells (see “Medicine is Moving from Calendars to Clocks” ) from a blood test. Both these immune system assessments are now moving towards commercial availability. The current study represents a 3rd path. In short, we’re getting there! NB. I wrote this post. articles.headline: 7 Chinese fashion brands changing what Made in China means
articles.dek: Still think Made in China means cheap? Tell that to the designer behind Rihanna’s Met Gala cape.

blocks.alt: 7 Chinese fashion brands changing what Made in China means

blocks.text: Chinese fashion: Key takeaways
• Chinese fashion brands are turning Made in China from a manufacturing label into a marker of design, craft and innovation
• Labels including Guo Pei, ICICLE and Uma Wang show there is no single formula for building Chinese luxury at home or abroad

When I was growing up, Made in China told clothes shoppers where something had been assembled. The tag signified scale and speed, low prices, and poor quality. The imagination behind the designs was never mentioned.

This is all changing. Chinese brands are in the ascendant. Homegrown fashion labels now show on prestigious runways and share wardrobe space next to global luxury’s biggest names. These are seven of the brands you should know if you’re watching that shift.
Guo Pei 郭培
Turning Chinese craft into haute couture

Guo Pei (郭培) established Rose Studio in Beijing in 1997. Back then, China barely had a modern couture industry. Her embroidered, architectural gowns have since entered international museums and Paris couture.

Rihanna’s enormous yellow Met Gala cape was hers, and that won the brand major attention. But Guo Pei’s biggest achievement has been building an atelier that kept its aesthetic Chinese-ness even when stepping out into the global market.
ICICLE (之禾)
Making the factory part of the luxury story

ICICLE offers the clearest reversal of old made-in-China narrative, in that their proposition rests heavily on Chinese manufacturing as an expertise field. They put the whole production system on display, keeping their claims about natural fabrics transparent.

It’s a proposition that’s attracted a minority investment from Gucci owner Kering in April of this year – that’s 2026 if you’re reading this in the future, by which point ICICLE will likely have far outstripped their 200 stores across 140 Chinese cities.
Uma Wang (王汁)
Proving Chinese fashion need not perform Chineseness

Uma Wang built her reputation through textiles and subdued colour – a style notably free of the obvious national symbols. The label was established in 2009 and went on to become the first Chinese designer brand to enter Milan Fashion Week’s official calendar. It then joined Paris in 2017.

Her success expanded the definition of Chinese design. International recognition no longer depended on conspicuous dragons, knots or other immediately legible cultural motifs. The authority came from the clothes themselves, and what went into making them.
Feng Chen Wang (王逢陈)
Putting craft into conceptual menswear

Feng Chen Wang uses deconstruction and technical outerwear to carry techniques and materials associated with her Fujian upbringing. Bamboo, plant dyeing and regional craft have appeared throughout her collections. None of it feels like a gimmick either. Her stated ambition is to build an international Chinese luxury menswear brand while challenging stereotypes attached to Made in China.
Susan Fang (方妍楠)
Handwork meets technology

blocks.alt: chinese fashion
blocks.caption: Image: Rednote/SUSAN FANG

blocks.text: Susan Fang approaches luxury as material invention. Her signature Air-Weave textiles, air-pleating, sculptural macramé and 3D beading combine the hard, fiddly work of assembly with mathematical and digital processes.

The result complicates the separation between artisan and machine. As an example of how far Made in China has come, Fang shows how China’s technical manufacturing culture can produce experimentation, not just scale and speed.
SHUSHU/TONG
Data as a sales indicator

blocks.alt: chinese fashion
blocks.caption: Images: Rednote/SHUSHU/TONG

blocks.text: Founded in Shanghai by Liushu Lei (雷留树) and Yutong Jiang (蒋雨彤), SHUSHU/TONG built a house on girlish looks, bows and pleats. Tmall sales data then helped the founders identify enduring commercial styles and push in those directions. Recognition followed, as did the Paris showrooms that carried them abroad.

By late 2025, the label had more than 40 international stockists. You’re reading about it here because the data element demonstrates how China’s digital retail system now has the ability to sharpen a designer identity.
Songmont (山下有松)
Taking Chinese bags towards the mainstream

blocks.alt: chinese fashion
blocks.caption: Images: Rednote/Songmont山下有松

blocks.alt: chinese fashion
blocks.caption: Images: Rednote/Songmont山下有松

blocks.alt: chinese fashion
blocks.caption: Images: Rednote/Songmont山下有松

blocks.text: Songmont began in 2013 with a bag sewn by founder Fu Song’s mother. It now operates almost a dozen Chinese concept stores and sells functional leather bags internationally. The price point sits below European megabrands, but it’s the momentum that’s significant. If you’re looking for the posterchild of Chinese faith in their own luxury brands, look no further than Songmont.
The Dao view: Made in China becomes a luxury proposition

These brands are not following one Chinese luxury formula. Some revive endangered crafts, others emphasise manufacturing prowess or cultural confidence. Behind this is, of course, a wide and robust network of digital feedback and consumers whose definition of status is changing.

But the really important thing that ties them all together is that they don’t water down their Chinese-ness for the global market. Really, they lean into it. Chinese heritage – though it lacks the recognition and mythology of European and American fashion houses – has emerged as something global consumers are willing to pay luxury prices for. Made in China is the source of that value, no longer a country-of-origin tag.
Source: DAO Insights — https://daoinsights.com/works/chinese-fashion-brands/

articles.headline: World’s first fighting robot league: humanoid T800s battle in Riyadh
articles.dek: Introducing CyberHero, from RADII’s weekly newsletter

blocks.alt: Robots Are Now Fighting for Their Spot in the Sports World

blocks.text: If you thought the future of sports was going to involve humans getting faster, stronger, and more genetically optimized, think again. Just yesterday in Riyadh—Saudi Arabia’s capital—the athletes were made of full metal.

blocks.alt: RADII highlights Hero esports' CyberHero robot fighting league in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia.

blocks.text: CyberHero, billed as the world’s first global humanoid robot sports league, officially launched in the vibrant city with a spectacle that looked like someone had mashed together a boxing match, an esports tournament, and a sci-fi movie (think Hugh Jackman’s Real Steel)—then given the whole thing a giant entertainment budget.

blocks.alt: RADII highlights Hero esports' CyberHero robot fighting league in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia.
blocks.caption: Scene from Real Steel (2011), back when fighting humanoid robots was a mere sci-fi fantasy. Image via YouTube/Prime Recap.

blocks.text: The event featured EngineAI T800 humanoid robots going head-to-head inside a purpose-built arena, marking the Middle East’s first humanoid robot combat event. Roughly 1.73 meters tall and weighing between 75 and 85 kilograms, the T800s are about human-sized, except they come equipped with 29 articulated joints and the ability to walk, run, punch, kick, turn, and recover after taking a beating (or tumble). Apparently, they can dance, too (but so can we… Big whoop).

blocks.alt: RADII highlights Hero esports' CyberHero robot fighting league in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia.

blocks.text: Behind the new league and sci-fi-turned-reality spectacle is Hero Esports, one of Asia’s biggest esports operators, which organizes more than 7,000 esports competitions annually that reach more than 800 million fans worldwide. If you’re unfamiliar with the company, you’ll most likely have heard of some of its major titles, including Honor of Kings, Peacekeeper Elite, League of Legends, and VALORANT, as well as its role as a China partner of the Esports World Cup. Now it is betting that the next arena for competitive entertainment might not be digital at all.

blocks.alt: RADII highlights Hero esports' CyberHero robot fighting league in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia.
blocks.caption: Hero Esports is the primary partner and tournament organizer of Riot Games’ Valorant, a character-based tactical FPS. Image via HS Insider.

blocks.text: The plan is ambitious: eight CyberHero stops across four regions—the Middle East, Europe, the Americas, and Asia. Rather than keeping robots behind glass in research labs, Hero Esports wants to put them under bright lights, in front of crowds, and see what happens when competition becomes part of the development process.

“CyberHero was born from a bold idea about the future of competition: that robots can be pushed to test their limits, break new boundaries, and improve through data generated in competition,” said Danny Tang, Co-founder and CEO of Hero Esports.

blocks.alt: RADII highlights Hero esports' CyberHero robot fighting league in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia.
blocks.caption: A flashy flying kick from one of the T800 robots.

blocks.text: “That is one of the lessons we have learned from esports, and it is also a responsibility we see for Hero Esports over the next decade—to use competition to drive innovation and progress. We are now establishing a global technology lab at our Shanghai headquarters to bring together technical expertise and talent from around the world.”
That last part is important. The fighting is basically the flashy bit.

blocks.alt: RADII highlights Hero esports' CyberHero robot fighting league in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia.

blocks.text: CyberHero’s competition is built around three roles: builders, who design and engineer the robots (brings to mind Big Hero 6); coders, who develop and train the software that controls their intelligence; and drivers, who make live decisions during competition. Think BattleBots but swap out Roombas with spin blades for Power Ranger-looking humanoids.

blocks.alt: RADII highlights Hero esports' CyberHero robot fighting league in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia.
blocks.caption: Fighting “Doombas.” Image via BattleBot Wiki.

blocks.text: The concept also taps into one of the biggest shifts happening in robotics right now: “physical AI.” In simple terms, that means AI that doesn’t just generate text or images on a screen, but can perceive and act in the real world through a physical body. The better these systems become at balancing, navigating, reacting, and learning, the less humanoid robots look like fancy prototypes and the more they start looking like actual machines with jobs to do.

China has been particularly aggressive in turning that idea into public spectacle. Earlier this year, Shenzhen hosted the launch of URKL, a commercial humanoid robot fighting league using the same EngineAI T800 platform. And at Beijing’s 2026 World Humanoid Robot Games, robot athletes competed in everything from sprinting to jumping—with some machines even threatening human athletic records.

blocks.alt: RADII highlights Hero esports' CyberHero robot fighting league in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia.

blocks.text: RADII has been following this weird, fascinating transition for a while. In our recent piece “Faster Than Usain Bolt? Why China’s Running Robots Mean Plan B is Canceled,” we looked at what happens when humanoid machines start challenging the physical limits we once considered exclusively human.
We’ve also asked whether robot combat is actually the best use of all this rapidly developing technology in “Are Fighting Robots the Future? Inside the World’s First URKL Combat.”

blocks.alt: RADII highlights Hero esports' CyberHero robot fighting league in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia.

blocks.text: The question is becoming harder to avoid. What happens when robots stop being demonstrations and start becoming competitors?

At CyberHero x Riyadh, the answer was wrapped in lasers, music, and influencer culture. MENA creator AboFlah and Saudi sports creator Bashar Arabi served as team managers, while electronic producer and DJ Tokyo Machine supplied the soundtrack. The result was deliberately closer to a gaming event than a robotics conference—because if humanoid robots are going to become a new form of entertainment, they’ll need fandom, personalities, and a little bit of chaos along with their algorithms.

For now, the machines are still very much machines. They (hilaruously) fall over or go completely unhinged. They need batteries. They require teams of humans to build, program, and operate them. And unlike the athletes they’re trying to replace, they don’t get to complain about bad refereeing.

blocks.alt: RADII highlights Hero esports' CyberHero robot fighting league in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia.

blocks.text: But that may be precisely the point.

Sport has always been a way of testing what bodies can do. CyberHero is proposing a slightly stranger question: what can an artificial body learn to do when we give it a stadium, an equal rival, and a reason to win?
Riyadh may have just given us the first glimpse.
All images via Hero Esports unless stated otherwise.

articles.headline: How Chinese games are reaching the world
articles.dek: Levelup Games bridges Chinese-made titles to global audiences, by Richard Lai

blocks.alt: Meet the Shanghai Studio Quietly Rewiring How China’s Games Reach the World

blocks.text: Tucked into an office on a Shanghai street, a small team is trying to pull off something that’s tripped up companies with far bigger budgets: getting the rest of the world to actually care about Chinese-made games—without the story getting flattened into censorship headlines, “soft power” op-eds, or reductive Tencent comparisons.

Levelup Games hasn’t fully cracked this. Nobody has. But it’s got a burgeoning two-city setup, a clear point of view, and—somewhat improbably—a two-time Oscar-winning filmmaker quietly advising on narrative.

Founded in 2024, Levelup splits its dozen-or-so team members between Shanghai and LA. The category it’s chasing is a familiar one to anyone who’s spent time on the Chinese indie gaming scene over the past few years: pixel art, sims, city-builders, cozy RPGs—the genres that don’t dominate headlines but quietly build some of the most devoted communities on Bilibili, Steam, and Xiaohongshu. Co-founder and CEO Daniel Liu frames Levelup’s job as giving these games “the context, care, and respect” they deserve when they cross borders. It’s a polite way of saying that most cross-border publishing, in either direction, still kind of sucks at this.

Anyone who’s spent time in wuxia-sandbox Discord servers already knows The Scroll of Taiwu. This title by Kunming studio ConchShipGames has been in Early Access for eight years, moved more than three million copies, and built a cult following on the strength of its absurdly deep, generational sect-building systems—the kind of mechanical density that’s very much a guochan (domestically-made) flex, and not an easy sell to Western press used to more legible action-RPG structures.

Levelup didn’t build Taiwu. What it did was translate the game’s cultural density into something Western outlets could actually engage with, resulting in coverage from major game publications like PC Gamer and GamesIndustry.biz. It’s become Levelup’s go-to case study for what “China-to-global” publishing should look like: not sanding down the cultural specificity, but building the bridge so Western audiences don’t need a wiki page open just to appreciate what makes the game special.

The more interesting move, though, is what happened at Gamescom 2026, when Levelup showed up attached to Murals. It’s the new isometric action game from British studio Dlala Studios of Disney Illusion Island and the Battletoads reboot, with composer David Housden—who scored both those games—back for a full live-orchestra score this time around. Polygon called it “the coolest new action game of Gamescom 2026,” praising a combat loop with real roguelike flavor. Though Dlala is careful to point out Murals is fully linear, not an actual roguelike that’s wrapped around a genuinely unsettling, hand-painted fairy-tale aesthetic. The studio’s own reference point is Who Framed Roger Rabbit, with its hand-painted 2D environments colliding with fully-modeled 3D combat, held together so the seams don’t show. Familiar stories—Sleeping Beauty, Rapunzel, Hansel and Gretel—get turned inside out, with recognizable characters recast as enemies. Basically nothing from your childhood is safe. (The name checks out, too: the hero’s only companion, Loaf, is literally a sketch that’s come to life; a mural that’s wandered off the wall.)

Levelup’s involvement started as a straightforward China-market localization deal and, per CEO Daniel Liu, has since grown into broader APAC publishing support. The stakes here are higher than they might look at first glance: Murals is Dlala’s first wholly original IP in over a decade, and the first title the studio is self-publishing rather than routing through a larger partner. That makes outfits like Levelup, who handles China-region strategy, and Tara Bruno PR, who runs general press, less of a nice-to-have and more like infrastructure Dlala doesn’t yet have in-house. It’s a quieter signal than the Taiwu case, but arguably a more important one: a Chinese company doing inbound cultural translation work—not just outbound. For a studio built on the premise that cross-border publishing shouldn’t just run in one direction, it’s the proof point that matters most.

blocks.caption: Dlala Studios and LevelUp Games at Gamescom 2026.

blocks.text: The Levelup team itself reads like a deliberate answer to where most publishers screw this up. Co-founder Rupert Zhao spent years as a gaming journalist, which shows in how fluently Levelup talks to press instead of at them. COO Selina Sun’s management-consulting background explains the company’s fondness for phrases like “commercial conversion” in its decks. And then there’s advisor Malcolm Clarke—a four-time Oscar nominee, two-time winner—offering narrative guidance to a slate of pixel-art farm sims and fairytale horror games, which is either a slightly absurd flex or exactly the instinct a cozy-games publisher needs to make sure the vibes hold up under scrutiny.

Liu, for his part, resists being boxed into the “helping foreign games break into China” narrative that a lot of outlets default to. “I wouldn’t frame Levelup purely as a global-to-China play,” he says. Levelup, in his telling, is “a cross-border publishing company that can work effectively in both directions.” His bio leans into the joke a little: an “investor-trained entrepreneur who turned a love for pixel art into a publishing company,” on a mission of “convincing people that cozy games are a legitimate asset class.”

Indeed, cozy games have become one of the most reliable engines of loyal, low-churn player bases anywhere. A genre built for people who are burnt out on live-service treadmills and gacha FOMO—Chinese and Western players alike. Levelup’s current slate—Everholm‘s slow-burn island mystery, Firefly Village‘s pocket-sized farming loop, Shrine’s Legacy‘s 16-bit co-op throwback, Can’t Stop Rory‘s farming-by-day-mecha-by-night hybrid—reads less like a random indie catalogue and more like a coherent bet on where a meaningful slice of the global player base is already heading.

None of this makes Levelup a major player yet. It’s a small team making calculated bets in an industry still figuring out how to talk about Chinese games without either overselling the soft-power narrative or reducing everything to a geopolitics story. But the Taiwu-to-Murals arc, compressed into about eighteen months, says something real about where cross-border publishing could actually go: less about which direction the export flows, and more about whether anyone’s doing the actual work of translation—culturally, not just linguistically—in either direction.
That’s a smaller story than “China’s gaming industry flexes soft power abroad.” It’s also a more useful one.

blocks.text: Les chiffres publiés ces derniers jours par BAK Economics sont particulièrement éloquents : en Suisse occidentale, les sciences de la vie représentent CHF 28,3 milliards d’impact économique, plus de 83’000 emplois directs et indirects, près de 30 % de la valeur ajoutée nationale du secteur, 36 % des brevets suisses en sciences de la vie et plus de CHF 10,5 milliards de capital-risque attirés entre 2020 et 2024.
Ces chiffres montrent une chose : les sciences de la vie ne sont pas seulement un secteur important. Elles sont devenues l’un des piliers de notre économie régionale et nationale.
Mais précisément parce que cet écosystème est fort, nous ne devons pas le considérer comme acquis.
À l’occasion des 25 ans de la Health Valley, nous organisons le 27 novembre prochain, de 09h00 à 13h00 à l’IMD à Lausanne, une matinée de réflexion stratégique consacrée à une question simple :

Qu’avons-nous construit, qu’est-ce qui est aujourd’hui sous pression et que devons-nous absolument préserver pour que la Suisse reste une place majeure des sciences de la vie dans les 25 prochaines années ?

La rencontre réunira dirigeants industriels, responsables politiques, entrepreneurs, investisseurs et acteurs académiques pour confronter les points de vue sur la compétitivité, l’attractivité, l’innovation, les talents, la production, la recherche clinique et les investissements.

L’objectif n’est pas de célébrer ce qui a été accompli, mais de nous demander collectivement ce que nous devons faire pour que les entreprises puissent continuer à innover, investir et se développer en Suisse.
Je serais très heureux de pouvoir vous compter parmi nous le 27 novembre.
Bien cordialement,
Benoît Dubuis

articles.dek: Benedict’s Newsletter No. 664: who gets to own the customer when agents do the shopping

blocks.alt: A person walking down an aisle between supercomputer racks

blocks.text: Agent incentives

Agents remain super hot, even if Muse and especially Instinct look an awful lot like the fever-brain excitement around Clubhouse in the pandemic. But if they are going to work, lots of other things need to be plugged together, most obviously how they actually talk to other websites and each other. Meta has launched a new standard (‘Personal Agent Protocol’) with the bunch of logos on the slide. Standards, of course, are one of the key strategic weapons when tech ecosystems try to go to war, and it’s always notable who isn’t on the list, and important to remember that getting the partnership person to sign a partnership deal is not the same as getting the company to use the partnership.

Meanwhile, Amazon and a bunch of other retailers are blocking agents entirely. This is partly short-term concern around fraud chargebacks and liability, and it’s not irrational for them to press pause until they worked out how to manage this more generally. There’s a 20-year-old and 150-year-old question of customer ownership versus distribution. If you’re big and already have traffic, you want to own the experience and talk to the customer directly, and if you’re small, you’re willing to take distribution instead. The additional wrinkle, of course, is that Amazon did $75 billion of ad revenue in the last 12 months, and the agent doesn’t see the ads.

Open outside China

Since Meta abandoned Llama, most of the credible open source models have come from China, which skews the debate about open a fair bit, but now American startup Reflection has launched a pretty credible open model and Mistral, which everyone had forgotten about, has come back from France with a credible model of its own. The FT reports that Nvidia is looking at buying Reflection, as part of the Bank of Jensen strategy to accelerate AI adoption while fragmenting the customer base.

IPO overhang

I think there were two fundamental changes in AI this year: agentic coding achieved explosive product-market fit, and AI infrastructure capex outgrew the cash flows of the hyperscalers and had to go to the financial markets. There’s been an enormous amount of capital raising of every kind this year, and markets are starting to get uncomfortable: in the last quarter a whole bunch of IPOs were pulled, partly also due to the imminent Anthropic IPO crowding everything out.

articles.headline: AI and the future of Chinese e-commerce – an interview with HKU’s Professor Xi Li
articles.dek: Your next customer might send an algorithm to do the shopping. Will it fall for your advertising?

blocks.alt: DAO Insights illustration for the interview on AI and Chinese e-commerce

blocks.text: Xi Li (李曦) is a professor of marketing at the University of Hong Kong, where he studies how AI and algorithms influence businesses and consumers.
His academic career spans computer science at Tsinghua University, operations research at the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, and a management PhD at the University of Toronto.

His research covers online marketplaces, personalised pricing and consumer privacy. For Dao Insights, he discusses how AI shopping agents could reshape Chinese e-commerce, changing how brands reach customers and compete for their attention.
Where is AI already making the biggest difference to Chinese e-commerce?

At the present stage, I think AI is changing e-commerce mainly in two related ways. First, it is changing the process of product search. Previously, consumers had to define what they wanted in some detail before they could search for it.

If I was planning a trip, for example, I would first choose a destination and then look for a hotel. Now a consumer can simply say, ‘I want a seaside destination where I can dive and eat good seafood,’ and ask AI to recommend options, without first specifying the exact product. This makes search much more convenient. A field experiment on Meituan’s generative search found that this kind of intent-aware search increased purchases.

Second, in the future, users may not go directly to each shop or platform. They may instead compare options across platforms through AI. Returning to the hotel example, rather than checking Ctrip and Meituan separately, we may simply ask an AI tool to recommend a hotel that offers good value for money. This could divert traffic from traditional internet platforms and intensify competition between hotels. I believe this will happen, but there is not yet enough public data to say how large the broader cross-platform effect will be.
Are recommendation systems evolving into genuine shopping agents?

Recommendation systems will certainly change. The biggest change, as I mentioned, is that they make searching more convenient. Consumers no longer need to search through platforms one by one; they can put a question directly to an AI and ask it to help.

There is another benefit for consumers. In the past, they might not have known much about certain products. When buying a car battery, a medicine or another specialised product, for example, it can be difficult to judge which option is better, and consumers may spend a long time researching and comparing.

AI can help organise and compare the information, making it easier to assess value for money. This may make products with stronger objective features easier to identify. Before an AI can complete purchases on a consumer’s behalf, it would still need reliable product information and clear authorisation for payment. In the case of medicines, it should support rather than replace professional advice.
If consumers increasingly shop through AI assistants, how will products earn visibility?

This is what is often called GEO. Previously, we talked about SEO: making sure a search engine could find a product. Now companies also need to think about GEO, so that AI can retrieve and understand their products. GEO should not be treated as a complete replacement for SEO; the basic search principles still matter.

On the one hand, the underlying strength of the product becomes more important. Persuasive language may work with an individual consumer, but copywriting alone may be less useful to an AI agent. AI may also use different sources from those a consumer would normally consult. Companies may therefore need authoritative endorsements, objective product specifications, accurate availability information and clear answers to frequently asked questions. In other words, they need to optimise their visibility in a different way.
What will this shift mean for merchants’ advertising strategies and costs?

The commercial model for AI is still not very clear, and we do not yet have one definitive set of lessons for companies. One likely development, however, is that some traffic will move from online platforms towards AI search interfaces. Paid recommendation is not yet a universal model: ChatGPT has introduced clearly labelled advertising, while Claude says it will remain ad-free. I would therefore not assume that every general-purpose AI tool will charge merchants simply to be recommended. Even so, if AI tools become important gateways for product discovery, they could divert traffic and advertising revenue from traditional platforms.

I do not think this will necessarily concentrate all traffic on leading products. Future AI agents may recommend different products to different consumers and make recommendations more personalised, allowing some long-tail goods to gain exposure. This could reduce competition for traditional advertising slots, although a small number of AI recommendations may also create a new kind of competition for placement.

Which businesses are best positioned to benefit from AI-led commerce? Will platforms and established brands gain the greatest advantage from their data, or could smaller merchants use AI to compete more effectively?

Following on from the previous question, I think products with good quality and clear objective information may be more likely to be favoured by AI, because AI relies more on product specifications and available evidence than on traditional persuasive language. However, AI can judge only from the data, reviews and other signals available to it; it cannot observe quality directly.

In addition, small merchants and long-tail products may have better opportunities, because AI can help people with niche interests find products that meet their needs. I see this as a possibility rather than an automatic outcome.
Is China’s deep integration an early indicator of where global e-commerce is heading, or are there features of the Chinese market that cannot easily be replicated elsewhere?

This is a complex question. In some respects, China may provide an early indication of where commerce is heading, for example in livestreaming and social media. Other features are not so easy to replicate. China has a mature logistics network that can deliver products to consumers very quickly.

China’s laws also differ from those in other countries, especially in Europe. Europe is generally more restrictive about the use of consumer data, although China also regulates personal information and automated decision-making. Some Chinese experience can therefore be applied in other regions, but it should not be transferred mechanically. Whether it is suitable depends on local conditions.
How could AI change the role of livestreamers, influencers and social-commerce content?
AI will affect content in two ways:
1. First, as you suggest, more virtual hosts and AIGC will appear online. They may replace some of the traffic previously generated by human presenters.

2. Second, traditional livestreamers have had to participate in person, but the time of leading presenters is limited and they cannot meet every brand’s needs. With AI, realistic livestream content based on an authorised digital version of a presenter can be produced without the person appearing every time. This could help leading livestreamers work with more brands and scale content production more quickly. Such content should be clearly labelled and used with the presenter’s consent.
Overall, I think virtual hosts will replace human livestreamers to some extent, but they will not replace the human market completely.
What new risks does AI introduce for consumers and brands?

There will certainly be many different problems, but we cannot yet identify all of them. They will need to be observed as the market develops. At present, I see four questions that could have a major impact:
1. Conflicts of interest and product quality. If an AI is paid to promote products, will that create a conflict of interest and lead it to recommend lower-quality products?
2. Merchant manipulation and consumer interests. How might companies use GEO, or generative engine optimisation, to make a platform recommend their products, and could this harm consumers?
3. Data privacy. To receive highly personalised recommendations, how much data should consumers share with AI?

4. Platform barriers and traffic allocation. Should internet platforms such as Amazon, JD.com and Taobao allow AI tools to access their data? If they do, does that mean handing their traffic over to AI?

At a minimum, platforms will need clearer labelling of paid recommendations, stronger checks on sellers and reviews, privacy controls, and a basic explanation of why a product was selected. The detailed rules will need to evolve with practice.

Chinese e-commerce companies are increasingly serving international markets. Could their experience with AI, logistics and highly integrated platforms give them an advantage overseas, and how might Western competitors respond?

Chinese companies are indeed further ahead in applying AI in some commerce scenarios than many overseas markets, especially in Europe, although American companies also have many innovations in AI applications.

I do not think China is ahead in every respect. Chinese and American companies have much to learn from each other, and this is a process of mutual learning. I believe more Western companies will draw on Chinese approaches in the future, while Chinese companies will also learn from Western approaches. The two sides will encourage each other’s development.
Looking ahead three to five years, what would convince you that agent-led shopping has genuinely arrived in China?

I believe that, over the next three to five years, more users will shop through AI agents. Consumers may become increasingly willing to do less research themselves before making a purchase and to delegate more decisions to an AI agent.

Products may also need to move from ‘to C’ to ‘to AI’. By this, I do not mean that consumers will stop mattering. Rather, brands need to understand not only how to design products that consumers like, but also how to make those products understandable and recommendable to AI. They may even need to think about how to present prices and offers to a consumer’s AI agent. These are important issues for companies to watch.
For platforms, the question is not only how to integrate AI into their own services, but also how to avoid handing all of their traffic to third-party AI tools. For example:
1. How can a platform ensure that its data is not accessed or used by AI without permission?
2. How can it create additional value that general-purpose AI tools cannot provide?

articles.headline: Chinese Football takes Chinese emo overseas
articles.dek: Moren Mao sits down with the cult-favorite Wuhan band

blocks.alt: Chinese Football: The Band Taking Chinese Emo Global

blocks.text: We all know how disappointing Chinese football—the sport—can be, from its inability to compete on the international stage to decades of corruption scandals. But Chinese Football, the band from Wuhan, is a different story.

Since releasing their self-titled debut album in 2015, the emo math-rock four-piece has won over fans worldwide. With signature cartoon-style album covers and a sound that remains largely distinctive in China’s alternative music landscape, Chinese Football has built a devoted following far beyond its hometown.
If American Football can be considered the pioneer of Midwestern emo, then Chinese Football has played a similar part in China’s own emo revival.

As for the band’s name, “It was just a joke,” frontman Xu Bo tells RADII. “When we formed the band, we never thought it would become our life’s work, so we didn’t put too much thought into the name.” Still, the association definitely comes with advantages. “Of course, we’ve benefited from having this name. We can’t deny that a lot of people first noticed Chinese Football because of it.”

blocks.caption: From left to right: Zheng Zili (drums); Wang Bo (guitar); Xu Bo (guitar & lead vocals); Li Lixing (bass & vocals).

blocks.text: Chinese Football’s self-titled debut opens with “Game Start,” offering a video game-inspired aesthetic that would become central to the band. Throughout the album and beyond, pop-punk riffs swagger in before giving way to uplifting math rock tunes; there is always a playful sense of rebellion.
When asked how they would define their sound, guitarist Wang Bo says, “We’re just making the music from our hearts.” Such a sentiment has carried Chinese Football through more than a decade together.

In 2017, the band released Here Comes a New Challenger!, the first installment of what would become its Game Trilogy. The albums created a meta-narrative centered around frontman Xu Bo trying to become a powerful rock star. Continue? Followed in 2019, before the full-length studio album Win&Lose completed the trilogy in 2022.
““This playground of life Satisfy all your imaginations” – Amusement Park Life, Win&Lose”

Across the trilogy, themes of adventure and the rollercoaster of life are framed through a language of video games. But beneath the playfulness lies Xu’s soft-spoken voice and a melancholy that follows adolescence into adulthood.
“In terms of our approach to making music, not much has changed,” Xu says. “We still follow the principle of moving ourselves first.”
Win, Lose, and Everything Between

Despite its praise, Chinese Football’s latest album, Win&Lose, drew criticism from longtime fans who saw the record as a shift toward a more pop-oriented sound. Xu explains that, compared to past works, Win&Lose is an album that focuses on expressing itself with lyrics and vocals. So it’s only natural that it’s going to be thought of as pop-leaning. Xu says, “We’ve always been making music we enjoy at the moment, and that has never changed.”
Drummer Zheng Zili offers an analogy.

“Not every French restaurant has to make escargot and foie gras, and not every Chinese restaurant has to keep making Mapo Tofu. Chefs create fusion dishes according to their own taste. No matter where the food comes from, the most important thing is that it tastes good.”

blocks.alt: RADII speaks with Chinese Football, emo math-rock band from Wuhan.

blocks.text: Chinese Football’s evolution has unfolded alongside major changes in China’s alternative music scene. When The Big Band premiered in 2019, it propelled previously underground acts into the national spotlight, while social media and short-form video further transformed how independent music reaches audiences. To get better insight, we asked CF what their thoughts are on the impact of these platforms.

RADII: We’ve previously reported on the rise of internet-famous bands, particularly after The Big Band went viral. What are your thoughts on independent music becoming more mainstream through the internet, music reality shows, and social media?

Li Lixin: Through reality television, independent music was seen for the first time by large audiences who don’t entirely understand underground music. Back then, if there were a hundred people who disliked you, you might never know. Now, if only ten people dislike you, you can probably find a hundred posts about it online.

For Xu Bo, visibility and genuine engagement remain two very different things. “A song might be seen by millions of people because of a ten-second clip,” he says, “but how many of those people will listen to the entire album, go to a live performance, or actually become part of the music scene?”

The internet has always been a powerful tool. Xu continues, “Growth through live performances and building an audience online don’t conflict. Because of the internet, we as a band from Wuhan, China, have had opportunities to perform in Japan, Korea, Southeast Asia, Europe, and North America.”
Defining the Chinese Emo Sound

If you grew up in the West, you probably remember the emo kids look: thick eyeliner, massive fringes, and My Chemical Romance blasting through their headphones. But you can’t say the same about China. Between an intense education system, strict dress codes, and a complicated relationship with counterculture, the emo boom of the 2000s never took off in quite the same way. There was the Shamate crowd, but that’s another story.
In the West, emo has experienced something of a renaissance in recent years, with genres such as emo rap taking off into the mainstream.
So what does emo revival look like in China?

Xu Bo: In recent years, you can clearly feel that emo in China, especially Midwest emo, has received more and more attention. In terms of cultural meaning and expression, however, it is no longer simply a continuation of Western emo from the 2000s. It has incorporated the emotional experiences shared by many young people in East Asia, including pressure, loneliness, and pain.

China may have missed previous waves of emo revivals, but this time around Chinese emo has developed much closer connections with the international music scene. Perhaps that has to do with the prevalence of the internet too.

blocks.alt: RADII speaks with Chinese Football, emo math-rock band from Wuhan.

blocks.text: From Wuhan to the World
Chinese Football will begin its highly anticipated second Americas tour this September. During the band’s first visit to the continent in 2024, nearly all 12 shows were sold out.

But Chinese Football has never set out to become a representation of Chinese music abroad. Bassist Li Lixin tells RADII, “We’ve actually never particularly thought about making some kind of so-called ‘Chinese music.’ Music itself is enough to create an emotional connection between people.” Li also notes the growing interest from the West in Asian music and culture: “Perhaps we can serve as a gateway for them to explore more Chinese independent music.”
RADII: If you could recommend some Chinese artists or bands to international audiences, who would they be?
Wang Bo: Fayzz, Duck Fight Goose, Fazi, Zhang Xingchan, and my personal project 温柔 D·BOY.

Xu Bo: Pu Shu and The Flowers had the greatest impact on me. I’d recommend that international audiences check out Chestnut Bakery, yourboyfriendsucks!, The White Tulips, Carsick Cars, P.K.14, Wang Wen, Default, The Three Mice, PostmodernHippie, and A Hidden Trace.

blocks.alt: RADII speaks with Chinese Football, emo math-rock band from Wuhan.
RADII speaks with Chinese Football, emo math-rock band from Wuhan.

blocks.text: In a 2023 interview with NME, Chinese Football said that its goal was “to break out of Asia and go to the world.” With that goal becoming realized, what comes next?
Zheng Zili: There’s a long road to walk between going somewhere and truly becoming part of that place.

Xu Bo: The world isn’t just Europe and North America. There are still so many places we want to go. For us, the next step isn’t simply performing in more countries. We want to truly enter more music scenes, meet more musicians, and connect with more audiences.

Chinese Football’s Occupy the Absence Tour will visit 21 cities in North America this autumn, with several dates already sold out. If you want to catch one of China’s most distinctive emo math-rock bands live, now is the best time to grab those tickets.

articles.dek: Shanghai Animation Film Studio, by Mia Fan

blocks.alt: How a Shanghai Film Studio Defined the Chinese Animated Aesthetic

blocks.text: If you grew up in China before the mid-2000s, chances are you’ve seen something produced by Shanghai Animation Film Studio. You may have wanted a magical brush like Ma Liang’s, capable of bringing anything you painted to life. Or perhaps you remember the unsettling world of The Rubik’s Cube Mansion (魔方大厦), where its young protagonist finds himself trapped inside a seemingly endless building.

blocks.caption: The Rubik’s Cube Mansion (魔方大厦, 1990–1994) became an unintentional childhood nightmare for a generation of Chinese viewers. Its surreal, imaginative settings evoke the impossible architecture of M. C. Escher’s Relativity (1953) and the fragmented geometry associated with Pablo Picasso’s Guernica (1937).

blocks.text: These were productions of Shanghai Animation Film Studio (SAFS), an institution often described today as China’s answer to Studio Ghibli. But long before such comparisons emerged, SAFS had already developed one of the most distinctive visual languages in Chinese animation.

blocks.caption: Nezha Conquers the Dragon King (哪吒闹海, 1979), with art direction by renowned Chinese painter Zhang Ding, who also contributed to the design of China’s national emblem in 1950. The film later became the first Chinese animated feature screened at the Cannes Film Festival.

blocks.text: Established as an independent studio in Shanghai in 1957, SAFS benefited from state support and was tasked with developing animation with a distinctly Chinese identity. But what exactly constitutes “Chinese aesthetics”? It is a very broad question, yet SAFS spent decades breaking it down into meticulously crafted moving images, broadcasting those aesthetics to generations of children.

blocks.caption: Many SAFS classics drew their stories from Chinese mythology, folklore, and classical literature, reimagining centuries-old narratives through animation. Still from The Ginseng Fruit (人参果, 1981), an adaptation from Journey to the West .

blocks.text: In an era when television itself was still a rarity for many Chinese families, SAFS created an entire open world for Sun Wukong in Uproar in Heaven (大闹天宫), the feature-length adaptation of Journey to the West produced between 1961 and 1964. Beyond its extraordinary scale and painstaking hand-drawn production, the film transformed Wukong’s rebellion against the celestial bureaucracy into a vivid story of resistance against authority.

The aesthetics could be just as radical. Color, composition, and character design drew from artistic traditions stretching back centuries. The Nine-Colored Deer (九色鹿), released in 1981, was adapted from the Deer King Jataka mural in Cave 257 of the Mogao Caves at Dunhuang. Its brilliant greens, reds, and earth tones, flattened landscapes, and decorative figures deliberately echo the visual language of the original murals rather than Western naturalism.

blocks.caption: The Deer King Jataka (鹿王本生图), a mural in Dunhuang’s Cave 257 and often described as one of China’s earliest examples of sequential storytelling. Image via Zhihu.

blocks.text: What makes SAFS productions so distinctive is this unselfconscious relationship with their own cultural inheritance. In The Nine-Colored Deer, physical realism is hardly the point. Mountains and water dissolve into one another; conventional linear perspective gives way to flattened, shifting spaces. Form serves spirit, rhythm, and harmony rather than anatomical or spatial realism. Instead of forcing Chinese stories into an imported visual system, SAFS allowed those stories to inhabit an artistic language of their own.

blocks.caption: Sloppy King (邋遢大王奇遇记, 1987) drew on real archaeological artefacts and ancient tombs to construct its fantastical underground rat kingdom. Photo via Xiaohongshu.

blocks.text: That confidence also produced remarkable experimentation. Across its early decades, the studio incorporated ink painting, paper cutting, folding, shadow-puppet traditions, opera, and folk art into animation. Pigsy Eats Watermelon (猪八戒吃西瓜) pioneered paper-cut animation in 1958, while Where Is Mama? helped establish ink-wash animation shortly afterward.

But the industry surrounding SAFS changed dramatically with China’s market reforms. As the studio faced increasing commercial pressure and competition from imported animation, the production model that had supported its labor-intensive artistic experimentation became harder to sustain. By the 1990s, the Chinese animation industry was operating under fundamentally different market conditions.

blocks.caption: Lotus Lantern (宝莲灯, 1999) marked SAFS’s push towards a new commercial era, combining traditional 2D animation with digital colouring and computer-assisted effects. Image via 1905.

blocks.text: Lotus Lantern (宝莲灯) became an ambitious response. Released in 1999, the feature assembled an unusually star-studded cast and soundtrack and represented SAFS’s attempt to create a commercially viable animated blockbuster. Yet in the following years, the studio gradually receded from the center of Chinese popular animation as the industry moved toward new production models and even more so toward 3D animation.

blocks.caption: Goose Mountain (鹅鹅鹅), an episode of the 2023 anthology Yao-Chinese Folktales, reimagines the ancient supernatural tale, The Scholar of Yangxian, through an eerie monochrome visual language punctuated by flashes of red. Still from Bilibili.

blocks.text: Then came Yao-Chinese Folktales (中国奇谭). Co-produced with Bilibili and released in 2023, its episodes moved between ink painting, folk aesthetics, contemporary life, and experimental visual languages rather than reproducing a single nostalgic “Chinese style.” One episode later became the basis for the feature film Nobody (浪浪山小妖怪). Released in 2025, the film became China’s highest-grossing domestic 2D animated feature at the time, earning more than 615 million RMB within weeks of release.

Whether this marks a brief revival or the beginning of another chapter for SAFS will depend not only on the studio and its animators, but also on the market and its audiences. Either way, its renewed visibility offers a reason to revisit the films of the last century—works that did more than entertain generations of Chinese children. They helped construct a visual vocabulary for what Chinese animation could be.
Cover Image via The Paper.
Source: RADII — https://radii.co/article/chinese-aesthetic-by-shanghai-animation-film-studio

blocks.alt: À Renens, l’Asinov School veut apprendre aux professionnels à travailler avec les robots humanoïdes

blocks.text: À Renens, une nouvelle école veut préparer les professionnels à l’arrivée des robots humanoïdes dans le monde du travail. Baptisée Asinov School, elle ne vise pas à former des ingénieurs capables de construire des robots, mais des personnes capables de les déployer, de définir leurs usages et d’organiser la collaboration entre humains et machines.

Le programme combine cours, projets pratiques et apprentissage par l’expérimentation. Il s’adresse aussi bien aux ingénieurs qu’aux professionnels de la santé, entrepreneurs, techniciens ou développeurs. Une partie du cursus peut passer par 42 Lausanne pour consolider les bases en programmation, avant un projet appliqué et une immersion d’une semaine à Shanghai sur des plateformes robotiques de nouvelle génération.

L’école veut répondre à un changement de fond : avec l’essor de l’intelligence artificielle « incarnée », les compétences recherchées ne concernent plus seulement le code ou la mécanique, mais aussi l’identification des bons cas d’usage, la supervision des systèmes autonomes et l’interaction homme-machine. Les secteurs visés vont de la santé à l’industrie, en passant par les services et le secteur public.

Asinov School est portée par la Fondation Inartis, avec des partenaires suisses et chinois comme la SATW, la Fondation Dalle Molle, 42 Lausanne, l’IDIAP, HEPIA ou encore le Unitree Shanghai University Institute.

blocks.text: The week in AI

Anthropic quietly updated its terms and conditions to say you’re not allowed to be “cruel” to its models. This is more of the anthropomorphism that seems like sensible speculation at a minimum to some AI researchers and insane to a lot of other people, as I wrote in my column last week. Meanwhile, it creates circularity problems - if you tell a model it has X characteristic, it will try to look like that.
Link — anthropic.com: https://www.anthropic.com/news/2026-usage-policy-update

OpenAI followed Anthropic in building a text watermarking system to comply with EU requirements. Unlike Anthropic, this is only applied in the EU, and OpenAI is also a lot clearer that they don’t think this is really a good idea: the tech is not reliable enough and too easy to work-around.
Link — openai.com: https://openai.com/index/eu-text-provenance/

Google launched Playground, an experimental space to use AI to generate your own games. AI is clearly going to transform both the economics of creating games (especially the hugely-expensive content creation of AAA games) and the mechanics of how games work (the NPCs can actually be intelligent now), as well as letting people spin-up improvised games like this. Compare mobile and app stores, and 3D.
Link — blog.google: https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/technology/ai/playground-experimental-gaming-platform/

Google launched a native Mac app that can connect to all of your software and take notes on what you’re working on, all running locally on-device. I don’t think it’s clear yet whether things like this are a feature or product, but meanwhile it is both predictable and hilarious that this looks nothing like a native Mac app, the download link doesn’t work in Safari, and the app is called “Google AI Edge Foresight”, which is exactly how Microsoft names products.
Link — developers.google.com: https://developers.google.com/edge/foresight
SpaceX Mobile

Following its earlier comments, SpaceX bought a portfolio of low-frequency cellular spectrum in the USA that would be needed to build an actual terrestrial network. US mobile operator stocks fell sharply. As I’ve I pointed out before, while SpaceX technology is extremely cool, satellite is either impractical or useless for the vast majority of real cellular use, and so if SpaceX actually wants to build a US mobile service, it will have to build what everyone else has built, spend more or less what anybody else would spend, charge more or less the same prices, and provide probably a mostly inferior service (the best sites are already taken). The most cynical interpretations remain that this is really leverage to get a good MVNO deal.
Link — bloomberg.com: https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-08/spacex-to-acquire-low-band-spectrum-for-mobile-phone-service
Apple as shadow ads regulator

Last month Apple briefly blocked one of the big ad network domains on iOS, and now there’s a wave of speculation that it’s working on a blacklist of a huge number of third-party targeting services, all of which allow advertisers to do terrible evil anti-democratic things to violate your human rights, like show you products you might be interested in and make money for independent publishers.

Apple here is an interesting example of what’s sometimes called a shadow regulator: it’s doing things that are really public policy rather than engineering or product decisions, but doing them without any due process, accountability or debate on devices used by well over half of Americans.
Link — adexchanger.com: https://www.adexchanger.com/privacy/apple-has-far-reaching-plans-to-block-hundreds-of-programmatic-data-companies-from-ios/
Ideas

A reminder to people who want to argue about whether LLMs could ever be conscious: our understanding of what consciousness really is remains so limited that we don’t even know if infants are conscious.
Link — nytimes.com: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/05/science/consciousness-brain-babies.html

An interesting piece by cryptographer Matthew Green on the history of law enforcement access to messages and encryption and how the coming wave of AI bug fixing might mean that law enforcement will no longer be able to hack your iPhone to get your messages and their visibility on criminal and terrorist comms will go dark.
Link — blog.cryptographyengineering.com: https://blog.cryptographyengineering.com/2026/08/14/everything-is-about-to-go-dark/
Satya Nadella wrote on his personal blog about liability when agents go wrong.
